tweets: On a tiny island off Mumbai's coast, a 20-foot stone face wears three expressions at once — carved into a cave sometime around the 6th century CE. No one agrees who commissioned it.
This is the Sadashiva panel in the main cave: one head, three faces — Aghora (destruction), Vamadeva (creation), Tatpurusha (preservation), carved directly from solid basalt rock.

There's no masonry here. Artisans cut INTO the mountain, removing stone to reveal temples, pillars, and sculpture from the rock itself — the same technique used at Ajanta and Ellora, but on an island reachable only by boat.

When Portuguese sailors arrived in the 1500s, they found a massive stone elephant guarding the shore — and renamed the island 'Elephanta.' That statue now stands in a Mumbai garden; the caves kept the name.

1,500 years later, Shiva's three faces still watch over the harbor, carved by hands history forgot to name. 🕉️ Follow @yddoseOfHistory for your daily dose of history.
